rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alif-lām marks class labels that apply to each member; this explains the definite collective in “from the people.”
rows.anchor: من كان من أمته أو كان في صفته من الأسماء التي يدخلها الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A common epithet can become a proper name for one person, as al-Ṣaʿq did; al-Najm likewise names the Pleiades.
rows.anchor: والصعق في الأصل صفة تقع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Ralān and Ibn Kurāʿ became names for particular men, so the names do not identify every son of those fathers.
rows.anchor: وكابن الصعق قولهم ابن رالان وابن كراع صار علما لإنسان واحد

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl says bare Zayd and ʿAmr name particular people; al-Ḥārith, al-Ḥasan, and al-ʿAbbās instead treat the person as the quality itself, while bare Ḥārith and ʿAbbās behave like Zayd.
rows.anchor: وزعم الخليل رحمه الله أنه إنما منعهم أن يدخلوا في هذه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stars al-Dabarān, al-Simāk, and al-ʿAyyūq retain alif-lām because each denotes a specific celestial object.
rows.anchor: فإنما يلزم الألف واللام من قبل أنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a star-name’s derivation is no longer known, Sibawayh attributes that gap to lost knowledge, not to a different naming rule.
rows.anchor: فإن كان عربيا نعرفه ولا نعرف الذي اشتق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Arbiʿāʾ and al-Thulāthāʾ mean “the fourth” and “the third,” yet function as established proper names like Zayd and ʿAmr.
rows.anchor: إنما يريد الرابع والثالث وكلها أخبارها كأخبار زيد وعمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dual forms such as two Zayds or two ʿAmrs remain indefinite when they mean any two people from those name-classes.
rows.anchor: زيدان منطلقان وهذان عمران منطلقان لم يكن هذا الكلام إلا نكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dual and plural place-names such as Abānān and ʿArafāt designate particular locations and are definite, unlike arbitrary duals of personal names.
rows.anchor: عرفات حسنة وهذان أبانان بينين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fixed places and mountains can bear such dual or plural names because they remain in place; people and animals move and can be distinguished one from another.
rows.anchor: وليس هذا في الأناسى ولا في الدواب إنما يكون هذا في الأماكن والجبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “the year of the two ʿUmars,” alif-lām makes the otherwise indefinite dual definite, like the well-known pair of stars.
rows.anchor: واما قولهم أعطيكم سنة العمرين فإنما أدخلت الألف واللام على عمرين وهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form faʿla can denote a kind or manner of action, as in qatlah and ṭaʿmah; Sibawayh distinguishes this use from a single occurrence.
rows.anchor: وذلك قولك حسن الطعمة وقتلته قتلة سوء وبئست الميتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same faʿla pattern does not always mean a kind of action: shidda, shaʿra, and duriya are lexical uses of the form.
rows.anchor: وقد تجئ الفعلة لا يراد بها هذا المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase layta shiʿrī is a frequent, lightened expression; frequent proverbs can likewise preserve forms that would otherwise sound heavy.
rows.anchor: وقالوا ليت شعري في هذا الموضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For one occurrence of an action, the regular form is faʿla directly from the verbal base, because augmented verbal nouns are not obligatory patterns for every verb.
rows.anchor: المرة الواحدة من الفعل جئت به أبدا على فعلة على الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A single occurrence can occasionally be expressed with an established verbal noun, as in itiyāna, liqāʾa, iʿṭāʾa, and istidrāja, but this is rare.
rows.anchor: وقالوا أتيته إتيانة ولقيته لقاءة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghazāh and ḥijjah name a single campaign or pilgrimage as lexical nouns rather than using the regular faʿla pattern.
rows.anchor: وقالوا غزاة فأرادوا عمل وجه واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qanmah, sahkah, and khamṭah are names for kinds of wind, not nouns formed from an action verb.
rows.anchor: وقالوا قنمة وسهكة وخمطة جعلوه اسما لبعض الريح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh conditions the construction after ḥattā on whether the entry is brought about by the journey, contrasting Zayd’s entry with sunrise and with baggage or the traveler’s body arriving.
rows.anchor: وذلك قولك سرت حتى يدخلها زيد إذا كان دخول زيد لم يؤده سيرك ولم يكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He treats arrival of one’s baggage or body as an event brought about by the journey, and compares it with entry that the journey has led to.
rows.anchor: ولكنك لو قلت سرت حتى يدخلها ثقلى وسرت حتى يدخلها بدنى

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Sibawayh reports Mujāhid reading “they were shaken until the Messenger says” with the Hijazi reading after ḥattā.
rows.anchor: بلغنا أن مجاهدا قرأ هذه الآية @QB@ وزلزلوا حتى يقول الرسول @QE@

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh permits coordinating another clause after repeated ḥattā; the second clause may be raised, as in the verse of Imruʾ al-Qays he cites.
rows.anchor: فهذه الآخرة هي ~~التي ترفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With one ḥattā shared across the coordination, raising “the sun rises” is not allowed, and making it subjunctive after a raised first verb is impossible.
rows.anchor: واعلم أنه لا يجوز سرت حتى أدخلها وتطلع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating ḥattā before the second clause avoids that problem, just as repeating a preposition can be good Arabic.
rows.anchor: ويحسن أن تقول سرت حتى تطلع الشمس وحتى أدخلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The coordinated “I traveled and he traveled until we enter” is understood as a joint journey, equivalent to saying “we traveled.”
rows.anchor: وتقول سرت وسار حتى ندخلها كأنك قلت سرنا حتى ندخلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Until I hear the call” takes the subjunctive because the journey does not cause hearing; dawn causes it, while travel can cause exhaustion and thus permits “until I tire.”
rows.anchor: حتى أسمع الأذان هذا وجهه وحده النصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Until I become morning” is likewise treated as a limit caused by sunrise, not by the traveler’s movement.
rows.anchor: أصبح لأن الإصباح لا يؤديه سيرك إنما هي غاية طلوع الشمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A lamented person is addressed with grief; the speaker may add a final alif for its drawn-out sound, and the form requires yā or wā before the name.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن المندوب مدعو ولكنه متفجع عليه فإن شئت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added alif opens the preceding vowel, whether it was kasra or ḍamma, because a letter before alif must be fatḥa.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن الألف التي تلحق المندوب تفتح كل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When possessive yā is attached, the final vowel is opened before the lamentative alif to avoid two consecutive sukūns.
rows.anchor: يا غلامي وقرأ يا عبادي قال وازيديا

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl allows waghulāmiyah: the yā can be made clear as in ordinary speech, and the pause hāʾ can clarify its vowel.
rows.anchor: في الندبة واغلاميه من قبل أنه قد يجوز

rows.speaker: ابن قيس الرقيات
rows.claim: Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyāt uses the lamentative form warazīyatih in his line about Salmā’s mourning.
rows.anchor: الشاعر وهو ابن قيس الرقيات # % تبكيهم دهماء معولة % وتقول سلمى وارزيتيه

rows.speaker: الخليل ويونس
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl and Yūnus accept both attaching and omitting the lamentative alif; the pause hāʾ disappears when speech continues.
rows.anchor: عربي فيما زعم الخليل رحمه الله ويونس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a possessive phrase such as “the breaking of my back,” the possessive yā remains because the word being lamented is not itself a direct vocative.
rows.anchor: وإنما لزمته الياء لأنه غير منادى

rows.speaker: رؤبة
rows.claim: Ruʾbah’s line is transmitted with two case forms for the lamented “father” and “sons.”
rows.anchor: ينشد على وجهين وهو قول رؤبة PageV02P222 # % فهى تنادى بأبى وابنيما % % ويروى بأبا وابناما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a noun’s own final yā meets possessive yā, the possessive yā is retained and opened; the lamentative alif remains optional.
rows.anchor: واعلم أنه إذا وافقت الياء الساكنة ياء الإضافة في النداء لم تحذف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif is optional in these forms; without a possessive yā, the first yā is deleted in wāmuthanāh to avoid two consecutive sukūns.
rows.anchor: إن شئت ألحقت الألف وإن لم تلحق جاز كما جاز ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥanānik means tenderness or mercy after tenderness; an implied verb such as “show mercy” is omitted because the expression has replaced it.
rows.anchor: حنانيك كأنه قال تحننا بعد تحنن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This apparent dual occurs only in an annexed construction and is fixed, like subḥāna Allāh and maʿādh Allāh.
rows.anchor: ولا يكون هذا مثنى إلا فى حال إضافة كما

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl reads the dual as repeated mercy: each moment of blessing should continue into another, making the expression emphatic.
rows.anchor: الخليل رحمه الله أن معنى التثنية أنه أراد

rows.speaker: طرفة بن العبد
rows.claim: Ṭarafa’s verse uses ḥanānik in an appeal for repeated mercy, illustrating the expression’s use.
rows.anchor: الشاعر وهو طرفة بن العبد # % أبا منذر أفنيت فأستبق بعضنا % % حنانيك بعض الشر أهون من بعض

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs say subḥāna Allāhi wa-ḥanānihi, meaning glorification of God and a plea for mercy; Sibawayh compares the form with rayḥānahu for provision.
rows.anchor: من العرب من يقول سبحان الله وحنانيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Labbayk and saʿdayk are fixed accusatives like subḥāna Allāh; their sense resembles the response “hearing and obedience.”
rows.anchor: وأما قولك لبيك وسعديك فانتصب هذا كما انتصب سبحان الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Labbayk and saʿdayk mean answering again and again and complying again and again; the doubled form intensifies the response.
rows.anchor: لبيك وسعديك إجابة بعد إجابة

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs use the nominative forms samaʿ and ḥanān, though the verbs governing those forms are not attested; samaʿan wa-ṭāʿatan is an accusative expression of compliance.
rows.anchor: ومن العرب من يقول سمع وطاعة أى أمرى سمع وطاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥadhārīk means “let there be caution after caution,” parallel to the repeated response in labbayk and saʿdayk.
rows.anchor: ومثل ذلك حذاريك كأنه قال ليكن منك حذر بعد حذر

rows.speaker: عبد بنى الحسحاس
rows.claim: The poet’s dawālik describes reciprocal, repeated action and can function as a circumstantial expression in the line about one garment being torn after another.
rows.anchor: قول الشاعر وهو عبد بنى الحسحاس # % إذا شق برد شق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ḍarban hādhā dhīka means this action after that one from each side; Sibawayh also allows a circumstantial analysis.
rows.anchor: ومثله أيضا # % ضربا هذا ذيك وطعنا وخضا

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus says labbayk is a single word in an annexed form, comparable to ʿalayk.
rows.anchor: لبيك اسم واحد ولكنه جاء

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl instead analyzes labbayk as a dual, like ḥawālayk, and cites the attested singular ḥanān as evidence.
rows.anchor: وزعم الخليل أنها تثنية بمنزلة حواليك لأنا سمعناهم

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs say lab or ḥawālik as shortened forms; the cited lines show that labbayk is not a preposition like ʿalayk, since its governing noun cannot be stated the same way.
rows.anchor: وبعض العرب يقول لب فيجريه مجرى أمس وغاق ولكن موضعه نصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh groups three conjugation patterns as shared by transitive and intransitive verbs, including faʿala-yafʿilu, faʿila-yafʿalu, and faʿala-yafʿulu.
rows.anchor: اعلم أنه يكون كل ما تعداك إلى غيرك على ثلاثة أبنية على فعل يفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Intransitive verbs have a fourth pattern, faʿula-yafʿulu, which transitive verbs do not share; Sibawayh says there is no transitive faʿultuhu.
rows.anchor: ضرب رابع لا يشركه فيه ما يتعداك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fourth pattern marks intransitivity; the other three past-tense patterns and their corresponding imperfect patterns are shared across transitive and intransitive verbs.
rows.anchor: فضروب الأفعال أربعة يجتمع في ثلاثة ما يتعداك وما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh lists ḥasiba-yaḥsabu among verbs with a nonstandard imperfect vowel; the fatḥa form is sound and more analogical.
rows.anchor: وذلك حسب يحسب ويئس ييئس ويبس ييبس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh cites al-Farazdaq’s line to attest the imperfect yanʿamu with ḍamma, describing guests’ delight or comfort.
rows.anchor: تنعم الأضياف عينا % وتصبح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A few verbs occur with ḍamma in the imperfect despite their usual pattern; Sibawayh gives faḍila-yafḍulu and māta-tamūtu and notes more analogical forms.
rows.anchor: وذلك فضل يفضل ومت تموت

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl calls the reported kāda-takādu pattern irregular, comparing it with the irregular faḍila-yafḍulu class.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول الخليل وهو شاذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For verbs with initial hamza, such as amara-yaʾmuru and akala-yaʾkulu, Sibawayh explains the imperfect vowel by analogy with assimilation and the treatment of a medial hamza.
rows.anchor: تقول أمر يأمر وأبق يأبق وأكل يأكل وأفل يأفل لأنها ساكنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also relates the following vowel to how a medial hamza and its counterparts would open a neighboring letter, while avoiding an opening that conflicts with a quiescent initial hamza.
rows.anchor: الذي قبل اللام فتحته اللام في قرأ يقرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh explains abā-yaʾbā by analogy with qaraʾa-yaqraʾu, while also allowing an analogy with ḥasiba-yaḥsabu.
rows.anchor: وقالوا أبى يأبى فشبهوه بيقرأ وفي يأبى وجه آخر أن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jabā-yajbā and qalā-yaqlā follow the qaraʾa pattern, but Sibawayh says these forms are known only from weakly transmitted usage.
rows.anchor: وقالوا جبى يجبى وقلى يقلى فشبهوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forms ʿamara-yaʿmuru and yaḥzuru follow the regular analogy; Sibawayh gives them as better-attested cases.
rows.anchor: وأما غير هذا فجاء على القياس مثل عمر يعمر ويعمر ويحزر ويحزر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sibawayh cites waʿadahu-yaʿiduhu as an analogy for opening after a quiescent initial radical, but says ʿaḍaḍtu-taʿaḍḍu is not well attested.
rows.anchor: وقالوا عضضت تعض فإنما يحتج بوعده

rows.speaker: أم سلمة
rows.claim: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet allowed pilgrims to leave ihram after stoning the Jamrah, except regarding women; if evening came before ṭawāf, they returned to ihram until circling the House. The excerpt gives no grading or link to 14:34.
rows.anchor: إِنَّ هَذَا يَوْمٌ رُخِّصَ لَكُمْ إِذَا أَنْتُمْ رَمَيْتُمُ الْجَمْرَةَ أَنْ تَحِلُّوا
